title: Spotting phishing and social engineering
summary: How attackers trick people by email, phone and chat, and what to do when something feels off.
body_md:
## What phishing looks like

Phishing is a message designed to make you click, pay, or share something you shouldn't. It arrives by email, SMS,
WhatsApp, phone calls and even video calls. Common patterns:

- **Urgency or fear**: "Your account will be suspended in 1 hour", "Payment overdue, legal action today".
- **Authority**: a message that appears to come from the CEO, a bank, a government department or IT support.
- **Unusual requests**: buy gift cards, change a vendor's bank details, approve an MFA prompt, share an OTP.
- **Look-alike links and senders**: `acme-support.co` instead of `acme.in`, or a display name that doesn't match
  the email address.
- **Unexpected attachments**: invoices, shipping notices or "scanned documents" you weren't expecting.

## Payment and bank-detail fraud

Attackers often impersonate a known vendor and ask to change bank details for future payments. **Always confirm
bank-detail changes by calling the vendor on a number you already have**, never one from the email.

## Phone and voice scams

A caller may claim to be from IT and ask you to install remote-access software, or read out an OTP. Our IT team
will never ask for your password or OTP. Hang up and call back through the official channel.

## What to do

1. **Pause.** Urgency is the attacker's main tool.
2. **Check** the sender's real address and hover over links before clicking.
3. **Verify** unusual requests through a different channel you trust.
4. **Report** the message with the "Report phishing" button or to the security channel, even if you already clicked.
   Reporting quickly after a click lets us contain the damage; you won't be blamed.

scenarios.subject: Mailbox full: verify within 24 hours or lose email
scenarios.body: Your mailbox has reached its limit. Incoming mail will be rejected. Click here to verify your account and increase storage: http://acme-helpdesk.co/verify
scenarios.explain: Urgency, a look-alike domain (acme-helpdesk.co, not your company's domain) and a sign-in link. Real IT teams don't ask you to verify accounts by email.

scenarios.subject: Notes from today's sprint review
scenarios.body: Hi team, notes from today are in the usual Confluence space under Sprint 42. Ping me if I missed anything.
scenarios.explain: A known colleague, your own domain, an expected topic, and it points you to a place you already use rather than a strange link.

scenarios.subject: Updated bank details for future payments
scenarios.body: Please note our bank account has changed due to an audit. Kindly update our details below before processing this month's invoice. This is urgent as the old account is frozen.
scenarios.explain: Bank-detail change requests are the most common payment fraud. Even if the sender looks right, call the supplier on a number you already have before changing anything.

scenarios.subject: Your payslip for September is ready
scenarios.body: Your payslip is available in the HR portal. Sign in as usual from the intranet to view it. We'll never ask for your password by email.
scenarios.explain: It tells you to go to the portal yourself instead of clicking a link, and the sender is your own payroll address.

quiz.q: An email from "CEO" asks you to urgently buy gift cards and send the codes. What do you do?
options: Buy them quickly; the CEO is waiting
Reply asking for more details
Verify through a different, trusted channel and report the email to security
Forward it to colleagues to see if they got it too

quiz.q: A vendor emails new bank details for future payments. What's the safe way to confirm?
options: Reply to the email to confirm
Call the vendor on a number you already have on record
Call the number given in the email
Update the details; vendors change banks often

quiz.q: You clicked a link in a suspicious email and entered your password. What now?
options: Do nothing; maybe it was fine
Report it to security immediately and change your password
Delete the email so nobody knows
Wait to see if anything happens

quiz.q: Which sender address is most likely a phishing attempt for a company using acme.in?
options: priya@acme.in
it-helpdesk@acme-in-support.com
payroll@acme.in
noreply@acme.in

quiz.q: A caller says they're from IT and asks for the OTP you just received. What should you do?
options: Read it out; IT needs it to fix your account
Hang up and contact IT through the official channel
Send it by chat instead
Give only the first three digits
